Teleoperation video · 5G field investigation · 4 September 2026

The Silent Downscale

WebRTC discarded seven eighths of the pixels in every loaded run — within one second, with zero packet loss and no drop in delivered bitrate. Nothing in either machine's logging would have shown it.

5 paired runs · 17,270 frames Host A → LiveKit SFU → Host B PTP synced, tens of µs
Correction · 5 September 2026

Sections 03 and 04 are withdrawn. They attributed the collapse to WebRTC's bandwidth estimator falling in response to 5G delay spikes, and to the encoder shedding resolution to meet a falling bitrate target. The delivered bitrate in the run that argument rests on does not fall. It holds between 9.1 and 10.1 Mbps through every one of A3's resolution steps, from the first frame to the last. An encoder losing its bitrate allocation cannot spend a flat 10 Mbps while it happens.

The mechanism is now unestablished — not replaced with a different one. Later work narrowed it usefully without closing it: the encoder was never starved of bits, and the picture shrank while every signal its quality scaler is documented to respond to was healthy. Everything measured below is unaffected and stands as recorded: the staircase, its timing, the five-second cadence, the zero packet loss, and the finding that the load ladder was never a ladder. What has been withdrawn is the explanation, and the redirection of the codec work that followed from it. Sections 03 and 07 carry the detail.

01What happened

The independent variable was never held constant

We ran a load ladder — three nominal resolutions, increasing offered load — to find where latency degrades. The ladder did not exist. Every loaded run held its configured resolution for a handful of frames and then collapsed, and stayed collapsed.

The two middle runs, nominally 640×360 and 960×540, both spent most of their duration at 320×180 — A1 for 3,323 of 3,475 frames, A2 for 2,780 of 3,463, A2 alternating up to 480×268 and back on a five-second cycle. They were not two load points. They were the same experiment run twice — which is why their numbers looked so similar, a similarity we had misread as the encoder gracefully absorbing the increase.

That divided by a spot uplink reading this report no longer stands behind; the ratio between two delivered bitrates needs no such assumption and makes the same point.)

03What the mechanism is not

The bitrate held flat through every step, which contradicts the explanation this section used to give

This section argued that 5G delay spikes drove WebRTC's delay-based estimator down, and that the encoder shed resolution to meet a falling bitrate target. The first half may well be true. The second half is contradicted by the run it was built on.

A3 steps its picture down four times. Its delivered bitrate does not move. What rises, monotonically, is the number of bits spent on each pixel:

A3 · elapsedDelivered bitrateModal resolutionBits per pixel
0–5 s8.16 Mbps1280×7200.30
5–10 s11.86 Mbps960×5400.76
10–15 s9.94 Mbps640×3601.44
15–95 s9.13 – 10.07 Mbps640×3601.32 – 1.46
95–115 s7.72 – 8.43 Mbps480×2682.00 – 2.18

An encoder that is losing its bitrate allocation cannot spend a flat 10 Mbps while it happens. Whatever drove the staircase, a collapsing bandwidth estimate is not visible in this run.

The sharper version of the unknown

The encoder was never starved. It held its target, the link carried it, no packets were lost, and the bytes were real coded picture. WebRTC's quality scaler steps down on high quantiser — and constant-bitrate encoding at 10 Mbps on trivially compressible content drives the quantiser low, which should have held the resolution or raised it.

So the picture stepped down four times, on an exact five-second clock, while every signal the scaler is documented to respond to was healthy. That is a more specific unknown than "the mechanism is unclear", and a more uncomfortable one: it says the trigger is something not yet identified, rather than something mismeasured. Settling it needs a repeat with the encoder's own quantiser column, which did not exist when these runs were made.

A later run shows the opposite signature

A separate 1080p run made two hours later, with the encoder's own columns logged, does match the withdrawn story exactly: bitrate falling 6.76 → 0.82 Mbps, bits per pixel flat at 0.2–0.3, quality_limitation_reason reading Bandwidth throughout, and QP pinned at the H.264 ceiling of 51 before every step — dropping to 48, 49, 44, 43, 35 immediately after each one. So the encoder does compress maximally first and shed resolution only when compression is exhausted. But that run happened on a collapsed uplink, and its signature is the inverse of A3's. Carrying its mechanism onto the A-series is the error this correction exists to undo.

The bytes were real picture, not padding. Padding is discarded at depacketization and never reaches the decoder, so decode time is an independent witness to how much actual coded data arrived — and across sixteen run-and-resolution cells spanning 1.5 to 49.4 kB per frame and five resolutions, decode time tracks bytes rather than pixels (r² = 0.81):

RunDelivered resolutionkB per frameDecode p50
Later 1080p run640×3606.10.87 ms
A3640×36041.13.93 ms
Later 1080p run480×2684.20.43 ms
A2-off480×26837.12.96 ms

Same resolution, same decoder, same source: A3's frames carry nearly seven times the bytes and cost four and a half times the decode. The one alternative that survived that test was filler emitted inside the bitstream by the hardware encoder, which unlike RTP padding would reach the decoder. It is ruled out too. NVENC inserts filler only when enableFillerDataInsertion is set, and the flag is never assigned anywhere in the SDK's encoder sources — it appears only in the vendor header that declares it.

What the encoder configuration does explain is the byte counts. It runs in constant-bitrate mode, with the average rate driven straight from WebRTC's allocation. Denied filler as a way to reach that target, an encoder has one remaining lever: lower the quantiser until the budget is spent on real detail. So on scrolling colour bars at a 10 Mbps target it produces 10 Mbps of genuine coded picture, because that is what it was told to do. Every figure above follows arithmetically — the flat bitrate is CBR holding a target that is a floor rather than a ceiling, the climbing bits per pixel is the same budget divided among fewer pixels, and A3's frames outweighing the later run's at identical resolution is simply the ratio of their two targets. At 2.00 bits per pixel the encoder was operating near losslessly on colour bars.

RunFirst transport spikeFirst resolution dropSpikes before the dropInterval
A10.00 s0.77 s18+0.77 s
A20.00 s0.40 s9+0.40 s
A30.00 s0.60 s10+0.60 s

Two notes on reading this. The spike column is every frame that arrived before the drop, not a subset: taking a spike as any sample above twice the run's median transport, all 18, all 9 and all 10 qualify. There is no quiet interval preceding the collapse in any run.

And these times are on the capture clock, not the receiver's. An earlier version of this table used arrival times, which inflated A3 from 0.60 s to 1.05 s by adding that moment's transport delay. The encoder's decision is made on the sender's timeline, so the sender's clock is the right one — and the difference between the two bases, up to 0.45 s, is larger than the quantity being reported.

It does not settle at a floor — it oscillates

The withdrawn version of this section said the resolution reaches a floor and stays there. It does not. A2 alternates between 320×180 and 480×268 six times over its run, and A2-off twice, on intervals of 5.00 seconds measured to the hundredth across eight consecutive steps. A3 steps down again at 96 seconds. The picture never returns to anything near nominal, which is the part that matters operationally — but the scaler is plainly still trying, and a description that has it giving up is wrong about what it is doing.

The measurement ate its own evidence

We excluded the first 90 frames of every run from the stall analysis as “startup artifacts,” because the publisher's frame cadence is genuinely irregular there. Those excluded frames are exactly the ones that trigger the permanent collapse. The filter removed the cause of the largest problem in the programme.

It removed most of the latency evidence with it, and it did so asymmetrically. Taking the worst 1% of frames by transport in each run and asking how many fell inside the excluded window:

RunWorst-1% frames inside the excluded window
Run B (control)0 / 35 — 0%
A2-off3 / 33 — 9%
A19 / 34 — 26%
A229 / 34 — 85%
A329 / 34 — 85%

The filter took 85% of the tail out of the two runs whose collapse we were trying to explain, and none of it out of the control. A filter that discards more evidence from the treatment than from the control is not removing noise, it is removing signal — and every comparison drawn across it was biased in the direction that made the loaded runs look calmer than they were.

04What this means for the production feed

1600×1300 · 30 fps · ~10 Mbps

The production video is 1600×1300 — 2.08 megapixels, essentially identical to the 2.07 of the 1920×1080 run. On this link, that run reached 640×360 within 11.03 seconds and held it for 2,536 frames, then stepped down again to 480×268 at 96 seconds.

An operator would be driving on one ninth of the intended pixels within eleven seconds of every session — 640×360 in place of 1920×1080 — with no packet loss and no drop in the bitrate being delivered.

The redirect is withdrawn with the mechanism

This box previously concluded that the congestion controller, not the pipe, was the binding constraint on resolution, and that the codec plan was therefore aimed at the wrong problem. That conclusion rested entirely on section 03, and section 03 is withdrawn. Naming the congestion controller as the culprit is not supported by a run whose bitrate never fell.

What survives is narrower and still worth acting on: the feed does not hold its configured resolution on this link, and nothing in the existing logging would have told you. That is a reason to instrument before choosing a codec, not a reason to have chosen a different one. Deciding between codec work and rate-control work requires knowing why the picture shrank, and we do not yet know.

05The five reports

Generated by run_report.sh — every one passes its clock check

These are the per-run latency reports, in load order. Each pairs the publisher and subscriber CSVs by frame ID and validates the cross-machine clock before reporting transport. None of them can show the resolution collapse — generate_frame_report.py has no reference to frame dimensions; it predates the column that caught this.

06Is the data trustworthy?

What was validated, and how

Transport is measured across two machines, so its error is the offset between their clocks. Both hosts are disciplined by PTP over a dedicated Ethernet cable that carries no video — the timing path is deliberately kept off the measured path, so congestion cannot move the clocks and the latency together.

The two hosts are not on the same timestamping tier, and that sets the real error bound. The subscriber timestamps in hardware; the publisher's NIC reports no PTP hardware clock and so timestamps in software. The measured path delay across the cable reflects it — a median of 74.6 µs over 27,851 samples, where two hardware-timestamped ends on a direct cable would sit in the single digits. PTP corrects for delay by assuming the two directions are symmetric, and any systematic asymmetry survives that correction as a constant offset. The servo's own report of a sub-microsecond offset is a statement about its precision, not its accuracy, and cannot see this. The honest bound is tens of microseconds — three orders below the smallest figure in this report, so nothing here changes, but it is the number to quote rather than the servo's.

RunPaired framesNegative samplesMin transportp50Max
Run B3,5440 (0.0%)18.95 ms32.11 ms96.01 ms
A13,4750 (0.0%)21.67 ms50.94 ms674.99 ms
A23,4630 (0.0%)21.27 ms49.00 ms1063.65 ms
A33,4460 (0.0%)22.19 ms50.46 ms1546.53 ms
A2-off3,3420 (0.0%)21.21 ms45.17 ms2365.80 ms

A negative sample would mean the receiving clock trails the sender and every transport figure is shifted. A minimum near zero would mean it leads, understating transport. Neither appears: the floor sits at 19–22 ms in all five runs, which is where 5G one-way latency belongs. Clock sync is not a limiting factor on any number here.

The link capacity figure is not solid, and an earlier version leaned on it

Uplink capacity was a spot reading taken beside the runs, not during them, and later work showed the link moves under it. A repeated probe on the subscriber's modem swung 2.4× — 12.8, 5.7, 13.7, 9.8 Mbps — within minutes with nothing changed, and the publisher's uplink separately fell to 0.14 Mbps and stayed there for over an hour. Before believing any of that, the probe itself was checked three ways: payload size (2, 4 and 8 MB give 13.7, 15.2 and 12.6 Mbps, so no slow-start truncation), pipe versus file (the pipe reads higher, so the upload path is not the bottleneck), and the entropy source (~3,800 Mbps, three orders clear).

So a single capacity number is a sample, not a level, and two samples taken at the ends of a run bound it only at those ends. This report no longer rests any claim on one. The measurement it does rest on is the delivered bitrate — 9.6 Mbps of real coded data arriving and decoding, held flat across every resolution step — which needs no assumption about what the link could have carried. Knowing the noise floor is 2.4× is also what makes the 70× gap between the two hosts' uplinks interpretable: a 2× difference would have been unreadable, and that one is not.

07What we got wrong

Recorded because the corrections were as informative as the results

  • “WebRTC's bandwidth estimate decays over a run.” Withdrawn. It was an artifact of probing with no subscriber attached — the estimator is a receiver-feedback loop, and with nothing subscribed there was no feedback to hold it up.
  • “The latency tail is driven by keyframes.” Withdrawn. The worst frames carry entirely normal packet spread; there is zero overlap between the transport outliers and the large frames.
  • “Stalls come from losing the uplink scheduling grant during idle periods.” Withdrawn. It predicts that stalls follow quiet periods; measured, they follow elevated demand.
  • “Stalls get rarer as load rises.” Withdrawn. An off-by-one in the episode detector discarded a 155-frame stall because it began one frame before the analysis window. Corrected, the affected-frame share is flat at 5.1–5.7% across all three load points.
  • “The two metrics disagree.” They never did. One included the startup window and the other excluded it.
  • “The estimate falls and the encoder obeys.” Withdrawn, and it was this report's headline explanation. A3's delivered bitrate holds between 9.1 and 10.1 Mbps through all four of its resolution steps. Nothing fell.
  • “It settles at a floor and stays there.” Withdrawn. A2 steps back up six times and A2-off twice, alternating on a 5.00-second cycle. The scaler is still working; it just never gets near nominal.
  • “The source is incompressible noise, so the collapse may be an artifact.” Withdrawn, and it was the most comfortable available explanation. The A-series ran on animated colour bars — the noise pattern did not exist in the code until two hours after the last of those runs, and passing it would have failed argument parsing. Trivially compressible content was consuming 9.9 Mbps at 640×360.
  • “The uplink had capacity to spare.” Withdrawn as stated. It compared a delivered rate against a single spot capacity reading, and repeated probing later showed that reading moves 2.4× within minutes. The zero-packet-loss result stands on its own and does not need it.

Eight hypotheses died on evidence. Two patterns are worth more than any of the results:

Every result that survived had a control or a matched pair behind it, and every hypothesis that died was reasoned into without one.

The dominant failure was a claim travelling from the run where it was measured to a run where it was assumed. The encoder mechanism in section 03 is the clearest case: it is correct, it is well evidenced, and it was measured on a different run, on a different link, two hours later. Nothing about it was wrong except where it was applied — which is the hardest kind of error to see, because checking the claim confirms it every time.

08What we still don't know

Stated plainly, so nothing here is over-read

  • What triggers the step-down, given that nothing the scaler responds to was unhealthy. This is the open question the correction leaves, and it is the one worth funding. It needs a repeat with the encoder's quantiser and limitation-reason columns, which did not exist when these runs were made.
  • Whether constant-bitrate encoding is the right default here at all. The encoder spends its entire allocation whatever the content, so a still scene costs exactly as much uplink as a moving one. For a teleoperation feed that is arguably wanted. But it leaves no headroom on a link we have separately watched fall seventyfold, and variable-bitrate at the same average would buy the same picture for less. Nobody has revisited this default; it is recorded here because it interacts badly with the failure that prompted this report.
  • No run has ever delivered sustained high resolution, so no client-side latency figure in this programme describes the production feed. The 1080p decode samples that exist are the first handful of frames of a run, where the decoder is cold: 24.92 ms median across six frames, against 0.59 ms for 320×180 across 2,776. Those are not comparable, and the pipeline has never been measured in the state it would actually run in.
  • Each load point is a single run. A repeat of the lowest point produced 17 stall episodes against the original's 11, so within-condition variability is substantial.
  • We cannot yet separate the sender's pacer from the radio scheduler from the SFU. Distinguishing them needs sender-side pacer queue depth sampled far faster than either host currently logs.
  • Nothing here says the collapse is unavoidable. No attempt has yet been made to pin resolution, floor the bitrate, or configure the degradation preference — that is the obvious next experiment and it has not been run.

Host B (subscriber, Intel i5-14400T, software H.264 decode) · Host A (publisher, RTX 5070, NVENC) · LiveKit SFU on T-Mobile edge · uplink and downlink figures are single spot readings, not sustained levels. Resolution and bitrate columns added to the subscriber CSV on 4 September 2026; they are the only reason this was visible.
